children: It's about to get a lot easier for brokers to have side gigs, so long as they aren't investment-related. On Tuesday, the Securities and Exchange Commission approved the relaxing of rules requiring brokers to report outside business activities.

The brokerage industry's self-regulatory organization, Finra, had asked the SEC to approve narrowing the outside business activities that registered representatives of brokerage firms must report to only those that are investment related. Finra told the SEC that it wanted to exclude activities from reporting requirements that it had determined pose lower risk to the brokerage industry or the public, including bartending or refereeing sports games, according to the SEC's 72-page order.

Under the new framework, brokers who intend to participate in outside investment-related activities are required to provide prior written notice to their brokerage firm, and describe in detail the proposed transaction and the person's proposed role therein. If the transaction includes compensation, then the broker would also need to obtain prior written approval.
The new rules will exclude from coverage activities on behalf of an affiliate of a Finra member firm, certain personal real estate activities, and personal investments in non-securities.

The SEC order says Finra's rule changes are reasonably designed to focus brokerage firms' supervisory resources on the types of outside activities that are appropriately within their purview. "Importantly, the proposed rule change would not limit a [broker-dealer's] ability to impose more robust supervision of, or to condition, limit, or prohibit, as appropriate, outside activities at the member's discretion," the order says. "For example, a member may expand the scope of its assessment or implement additional appropriate safeguards, limitations, or prohibitions, beyond the minimum requirements established here."

A spokeswoman for Finra declined to comment. In a September 2025 blog post, Robert Colby, chief legal officer at Finra, said the organization intended to pursue changes to streamline requirements for brokers and firms. "By eliminating the needless reporting of unrelated activities, both the firms' compliance staff and Finra's regulatory team can better focus on addressing actual risks," he wrote.
Finra submitted its proposed rule change in January 2026. The changes will take effect at a later date that Finra has yet to announce.

Brokerage industry groups supported the changes. "We appreciate Finra's risk-based approach that seeks to reduce burdens associated with low-risk outside activities while requiring greater firm involvement and scrutiny over higher risk activities that have the potential of creating investor confusion or leading to harm," David T. Bellaire, general counsel at the Financial Services Institute, wrote in a February comment letter.
